title: Step Count: Binary GCD vs Euclidean Algorithm
description: Formal step count comparison between Binary GCD (Stein's algorithm) and the Euclidean algorithm. Proves Lamé's theorem (Euclidean steps ≤ O(log min(a,b))) and Binary GCD logarithmic bound (steps ≤ O(log a + log b)). All results fully verified, 0 sorries.

meta.author: Formalized in Lean 4
originalContributions: euclidSteps: step counting function for the Euclidean algorithm
binaryGcdSteps: step counting function for Binary GCD
Bridge lemma: euclidSteps(a,b) = euclideanSteps(max a b, min a b)
Proof of Lamé's theorem: Euclidean steps ≤ 2·log₂(min(a,b)) + 2
Proof of Binary GCD bound: steps ≤ 2·(log₂(a) + log₂(b)) + 2

overview.historicalContext: The Binary GCD algorithm was published by Josef Stein in 1967, though it was known earlier. On binary computers, it replaces the expensive division operations of the Euclidean algorithm with bit shifts and subtraction. Lamé proved in 1844 that the Euclidean algorithm takes at most 5d steps where d is the number of decimal digits of the smaller input — this was one of the first complexity analyses in computer science.
overview.problemStatement:
Compare the formal step counts of the Binary GCD algorithm and the Euclidean algorithm:
1. Define step counting functions for both algorithms
2. Compute concrete step counts for specific inputs
3. Prove logarithmic upper bounds on both step counts
4. Characterize the worst-case inputs (Fibonacci numbers for Euclidean)
overview.text: Formal step count comparison between Binary GCD and the Euclidean algorithm.
overview.proofStrategy:
1. Define recursive step counters matching the algorithm structure
2. Prove basic properties (symmetry, zero cases)
3. Use native_decide for concrete examples
4. State logarithmic bounds (Lamé for Euclidean, bit-length for Binary GCD)
keyInsights: Binary GCD uses more steps than Euclidean (roughly 2x) but each step is cheaper on binary hardware (bit shifts vs division)
Fibonacci consecutive pairs are worst-case for Euclidean: gcd(F_{n+1}, F_n) takes n steps
Binary GCD worst case is when both inputs are odd primes of similar size
The total cost model (steps × cost per step) favors Binary GCD for large multi-precision integers

sections.title: Euclidean Algorithm Step Count
sections.summary: Defines euclidSteps and proves base cases (zero inputs, divisibility).
sections.mathContext: The Euclidean algorithm: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b). Each mod operation counts as one step.

sections.title: Binary GCD Step Count
sections.summary: Defines binaryGcdSteps matching the four cases of Stein's algorithm.
sections.mathContext: Binary GCD cases: both even (extract 2), one even (drop 2), both odd (subtract and halve). Each case counts as one step.

sections.title: Concrete Step Counts
sections.summary: Computes step counts for gcd(12,8), gcd(21,15), gcd(100,37), gcd(89,55) via native_decide.
sections.mathContext: Fibonacci inputs (89,55) are worst-case for Euclidean (9 steps). Binary GCD uses 11 steps on the same input.

sections.title: Symmetry Proofs
sections.summary: Both step counts are symmetric: steps(a,b) = steps(b,a).
sections.mathContext: Symmetry follows from the symmetry of gcd: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,a).

sections.title: Logarithmic Bounds
sections.summary: Proves Lamé's theorem and the Binary GCD logarithmic bound (0 sorries).
sections.mathContext: Lamé (1844): Euclidean steps ≤ O(log min(a,b)). Binary GCD: steps ≤ O(log a + log b).

conclusion.summary: Fully verified step count analysis for Binary GCD vs Euclidean algorithm. Both logarithmic bounds proved: Lamé's theorem via bridge to GCDAlgorithmOQ01, Binary GCD bound via strong induction with log-decrease potential. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: The step counting infrastructure enables formal comparison of GCD algorithm variants. The concrete examples verify the expected behavior: Fibonacci inputs maximize Euclidean steps, while Binary GCD has more uniform behavior across input types.
openQuestions: Formalize the total cost model (steps × bit-operation cost)
Prove tight bounds: Euclidean ≤ 5·digits(min(a,b)) via Fibonacci
